sentences.text: The wood's dusk is seven minutes later than it should be for that latitude, that longitude, and that date.
It is not seven minutes later than sunset — that would be normal; every wood is later than sunset by some amount that depends on the canopy.
It is seven minutes later than *itself*.

Her grandfather had a hundred and forty pages of it, going back to when he took the job in 1961, and the whole of it is consistent to within about forty seconds, and the whole of it sits seven minutes behind the tables.
Forty seconds of scatter over sixty years is, in Sidonie's professional opinion, the most impressive thing in that notebook.
Nothing biological is that consistent.
Her own measurements since 2019 sit inside the same band and she has far better equipment than he ever had.
He had not discovered this.
That was the part that took Sidonie longest to get out of him.

He had gone to the man who had the job before him, a man called Pirlot, in about 1963, with two years of measurements and a great deal of excitement, and Pirlot had listened to the whole thing in his kitchen and then said: "Oui.
Sept minutes." And that was all he said, and he changed the subject, and he was not rude about it, and he never discussed it again in the eleven years before he died.
Sidonie's grandfather described that kitchen to her once and the description has stayed with her.
Pirlot at the table.
The two years of figures spread out on it.
An old forester looking at the work of a young one, recognising every column of it, and saying two words.
Her grandfather asked twice more over those years and got the same nothing.
So he did what anyone would do, which was to ask around, carefully, in a village where his family had not been for four generations and where he was therefore permanently new.

And what he found was that everybody over the age of about forty knew, that nobody would say how they knew, and that the subject was not exactly forbidden — it was worse than forbidden, it was *declined*.
People would go quiet, and be pleasant, and start talking about something else with real warmth, and there was nothing in it you could take offence at and no way at all to get past it.
He gave up in about 1971.
Not on the measurements.
He kept those up to the week he retired and for eleven years after it.
He gave up on the asking, which is a different thing, and Sidonie thinks the difference between those two is most of what she knows about him.
Sidonie did not give up, because she was twelve and because he told her about it in the summer she was twelve, which he has since admitted was not entirely an accident.
